title: Charlie Catches a Leprechaun

jokes.text: Dennis's opening plea: 'because of everyone's A.D.D., I know I'm gonna lose your attention in about three minutes, and Frank's gonna fall asleep.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is trying to give a business presentation to the gang.
jokes.punchline: He preemptively roasts Frank's narcoleptic tendencies and the gang's collective attention span before he even begins.
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny cold-open dynamic. Dennis's condescension toward the group, stated as clinical fact before anyone has done anything, is a solid character beat. The Frank prediction pays off immediately, which is well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I slept 26 hours last night.

jokes.text: Frank: 'No way. I slept 26 hours last night.' Dennis: 'You still seem very sleepy.'
jokes.setup: Frank confidently denies he'll fall asleep during the presentation, citing impossible sleep duration
jokes.punchline: Dennis deadpans that Frank still seems sleepy — the 26 hours is itself the absurd punchline within the setup
jokes.explanation: Two-layered joke: Frank's claim of 26 hours is already absurd, then Dennis's unfazed observation lands perfectly. Very economical and character-true.

jokes.text: Mac's response to the mobile bar: 'Is that like a car service thing where we pick people up and take them from bar to bar and jack up the prices?'
jokes.setup: Dennis presents his innovative mobile bar concept
jokes.punchline: Mac describes Uber/Lyft surge pricing exactly, but framed as a sleazy criminal scheme and treated as a fresh terrible idea
jokes.explanation: Rewatch bonus: This idea gets paid off repeatedly through the episode and is exactly what they end up doing. The gang accidentally invents Uber in the most criminal way possible — the irony is rich.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: he played the flute for some kids, and then he lured them into a cave somewhere, and he diddled them.

jokes.text: Frank: 'We need to serve an irresponsible amount of booze to people who are genetically predisposed to having alcohol problems. St. Patrick started that tradition, and that's why we celebrate him today.'
jokes.setup: Frank wants to 'honor ancient Irish traditions'
jokes.punchline: He invents a grotesque fake history where St. Patrick's legacy is alcoholism-enabling, delivered with complete conviction
jokes.explanation: Frank's confident, wrong historical revisionism is perfectly in character. The specific detail of 'genetically predisposed' is a dark escalation that elevates it above simple ignorance comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: He drove the kids out of Ireland. And then he molested 'em.

jokes.text: Charlie's St. Patrick history: 'He played the flute for some kids, and then he lured them into a cave somewhere, and he diddled them.'
jokes.setup: The gang debates what St. Patrick actually did
jokes.punchline: Charlie blends the Pied Piper myth with a horrific molestation accusation against a Catholic saint, delivered matter-of-factly
jokes.explanation: Charlie's confused mythology mashup is perfectly him — wrong in a very specific, confident way. Blending the Pied Piper with Catholic Church abuse scandal undercurrents is surprisingly sophisticated for a Charlie-brain joke. 'Diddled' is the perfect word choice.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I feel like, in the olden days of the Catholic Church, pedophiles were regarded as heroes.

jokes.text: Mac corrects Charlie: 'You got him mixed up with the Pied Piper.' Then Charlie immediately: 'St. Patrick didn't play the flute. He drove the kids out of Ireland. And then he molested 'em.'
jokes.setup: Mac tries to correct Charlie's mangled history
jokes.punchline: Charlie accepts the Pied Piper correction but keeps the molestation, now attributing it correctly to St. Patrick — the error is structural, not factual
jokes.explanation: Brilliant comedic structure: Mac's correction only fixes one wrong detail while Charlie seamlessly incorporates it, keeping the molestation accusation fully intact. The logic is airtight and absurd simultaneously. This is excellent Always Sunny writing — Charlie's brain works on its own consistent rules.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm, like, this close.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'If St. Patrick molested kids, he would be regarded as a scoundrel.' Frank: 'I feel like, in the olden days of the Catholic Church, pedophiles were regarded as heroes.'
jokes.setup: Dennis tries to inject reason into the molestation debate
jokes.punchline: Frank counters with a historically uncomfortable truth about the Catholic Church, presented as confident revisionist wisdom
jokes.explanation: Frank's line walks a razor's edge — it's a pointed social commentary on the Catholic Church abuse scandal disguised as ignorant bluster. The word 'heroes' does enormous work. Dennis playing straight man is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I don't even know if I've set up my glue traps for him yet.

jokes.text: Charlie declares he still wants to try to catch the leprechaun and that he's 'like, this close'
jokes.setup: Dennis tries to redirect to business; Charlie mentions the leprechaun as an alternative
jokes.punchline: 'I'm like, this close' — implying years of near-misses in pursuit of a fictional creature
jokes.explanation: Classic Charlie mythology — his absolute sincerity about the leprechaun sets up the entire episode's B-plot. 'This close' is funny because it implies a long, failed history. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Charlie mentions he hasn't set up his glue traps yet, mid-argument
jokes.setup: Everyone is arguing about business strategy
jokes.punchline: Charlie suddenly worries he forgot to set leprechaun glue traps, treating it as the urgent practical concern it is in his world
jokes.explanation: The mid-conversation panic about practical leprechaun-trapping logistics is a great character beat. Charlie's brain drifting to 'did I set the glue traps?' like it's checking if he left the stove on is perfectly him.

jokes.text: Actually... I might want to get myself a flute. / I was thinking the same thing. / Go get a flute! Everybody go get a flute!
jokes.setup: Dennis is trying to regain control of his presentation after the St. Patrick/Pied Piper tangent.
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie rediscover their enthusiasm for flutes (from the earlier molestation tangent) and Frank erupts into 'Everybody go get a flute!' — causing the whole room to abandon Dennis.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the flute from the Pied Piper conversation lands with perfect absurdist energy. Frank's 'Everybody go get a flute!' is the kind of sudden, illogical enthusiastic command that is a hallmark of IASIP at its best. Dennis is then shown utterly defeated — 'No, he's gone.' This is a tight, well-structured bit with a great escalating payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Top o' the morning, you filthy lads. I'm fixing to have a whale of a time in this here mobile pub.

jokes.text: Frank and Mac spontaneously decide to go get flutes, completely abandoning the meeting
jokes.setup: Mac misremembers that St. Patrick 'played the flute for some kids'
jokes.punchline: Both Frank and Mac decide they want flutes right now and simply leave, mid-meeting — 'Everybody go get a flute!'
jokes.explanation: 'Everybody go get a flute!' is a great rallying cry for absolutely nothing. The total collapse of the meeting because two adults decided to get flutes based on wrong historical information is classic Always Sunny chaos momentum.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Frank's 'Crazy Paddy' Irish stereotype character

jokes.text: Dennis explains the mobile bar plan to Frank: QR codes, apps, Facebook login, 30-second ad, then beer
jokes.setup: Dennis claims the new system is 'simpler than cash'
jokes.punchline: The 'simple' system requires a QR code scan, app download, Facebook login, watching an ad, then placing an online order — just to get a beer
jokes.explanation: Sharp tech-bro satire. Dennis's sincere belief that this is 'simpler than cash' is both a character joke and a broad observational joke about startup culture. Frank's confusion is the straight-man anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I brought my piece in case anybody gets out of line.

jokes.text: Frank: 'That seems insanely complicated. Why don't we just take cash?'
jokes.setup: Dennis lays out the elaborate digital payment ecosystem
jokes.punchline: Frank cuts to the obvious with perfect simplicity
jokes.explanation: Frank as the accidental voice of reason is a reliable Always Sunny dynamic. Maximum economy — it's the most logical response to Dennis's absurdity, which makes it funny.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: 'Cause beer's not a food. When was the last time you ate a beer?

jokes.text: Dee enters in full Crazy Paddy costume: 'Top o' the morning, you filthy lads. I'm fixing to have a whale of a time in this here mobile pub.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just pitched a sleek, modern, innovative experience
jokes.punchline: Dee appears in an offensive Irish stereotype costume, doing a terrible accent, calling everyone 'filthy lads'
jokes.explanation: Visual gag with great comedic timing. The whiplash from Dennis's Silicon Valley pitch to Dee in a leprechaun costume is sharp. 'Fixing to have a whale of a time' is a great absurd non-sequitur phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: When was the last time you drank paint?

jokes.text: Frank pulls a gun 'in case anybody gets out of line'
jokes.setup: Frank is told he'll be driving the mobile bar
jokes.punchline: Frank casually reveals he brought a firearm as standard business equipment
jokes.explanation: Frank's casual gun reveal is classic Frank — violence as a first resort. Very economical and character-true. Not surprising for the show but executed well.

jokes.text: Mac reveals he found a snake and green paint for St. Patrick's Day preparations
jokes.setup: Mac shows off his St. Paddy's contributions
jokes.punchline: He has a live snake and green paint — connected to half-remembered St. Patrick mythology — presented as sensible holiday prep
jokes.explanation: Mac's vague justification ('snakes were involved') and green paint for beer because 'beer's not a food' are both solid. The confident wrongness is very Mac.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: It's not bad.

jokes.text: Charlie's logic: 'Why not use food coloring?' / 'Beer's not a food.' / 'When was the last time you ate a beer?' / 'When was the last time you drank paint?'
jokes.setup: Mac suggests food coloring instead of paint for the beer
jokes.punchline: Charlie argues beer isn't food, then Mac flips it back — 'When was the last time you drank paint?' — implying Charlie has been drinking paint
jokes.explanation: Exceptional comedic economy. The exchange builds in perfect rhythm: Mac's reasonable question → Charlie's absurd logic → Mac's devastating flip that reveals Charlie has been drinking paint. All four lines land. The structure is airtight and character-perfect. 'When was the last time you drank paint?' is quotable and pays off immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: Is this, like, a car service thing?

jokes.text: Mac asks to see Charlie's tongue and it's visibly stained with paint — 'Oh, my God, dude! Oh, that shit's just disgusting!'
jokes.setup: 'When was the last time you drank paint?' — implying Charlie has been drinking paint
jokes.punchline: Charlie's green-stained tongue confirms it; Mac is physically revolted
jokes.explanation: The visual payoff of the paint tongue is well-earned. Mac's visceral disgust ('that shit's just disgusting') while Charlie says 'It's not bad' is a perfect cringe beat. Physical comedy inferred from dialogue.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No, it's not a goddamn car service. Why does everyone...

jokes.text: Charlie: 'It's not bad.' Mac: 'You can't drink paint.' Charlie: 'I know. I hear you.' Mac: 'You say that, but I don't think you're gonna stop.' Charlie: 'Yeah, I get it, though, man.'
jokes.setup: Mac tries to reason with Charlie about drinking paint
jokes.punchline: Charlie fully understands it's wrong, says so sincerely, but it's immediately clear he will absolutely continue drinking paint
jokes.explanation: Charlie's brand of acknowledgment-without-change is devastatingly character-specific. 'I hear you' / 'I know' / 'I get it, though' are three levels of Charlie pretending to understand while completely not changing. This is the character at his best — not dumb, just operating on a different plane entirely.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You get in that wagon right now or I'm gonna sock you a good one right in the kisser!

jokes.text: Mac's sad resignation: 'It's like the guy doesn't listen to us, man, when we're trying to get through to him. It's a bummer.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has just announced he's going to check the basement glue traps for leprechauns despite Mac telling him not to chase leprechauns.
jokes.punchline: Mac's weary, fatherly lament about Charlie 'not listening' — delivered as genuine therapeutic exasperation — after failing to stop him from chasing mythical creatures.
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat. Mac and Charlie's codependent dynamic is well-established, and Mac's sad acceptance is in character. But this is more connective tissue than a full joke — it doesn't have its own punchline so much as it's a character-sad-trombone moment.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: Oh, wait, so is this, like, a bang bus?

jokes.text: Dennis turns away a potential customer aggressively ('No, not you. Keep moving') while trying to recruit hip clientele
jokes.setup: Dennis is looking for 'hip, attractive clientele' for the Paddy Wagon
jokes.punchline: He immediately rejects a would-be customer without explanation — the irony of turning away business while trying to run a business
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis gatekeeping — he's running a failing bar on a holiday and still turning away customers based on appearance. Very character-specific but not a standout joke.

jokes.text: Customer asks: 'Is this like a car service thing? Can you take us to Center City?' Dennis: 'No, it's not a goddamn car service. Why does everyone...'
jokes.setup: Mac already asked if the Paddy Wagon was a car service in the opening scene
jokes.punchline: Random strangers off the street independently have the same idea — it IS obviously a car service, and Dennis's exasperation grows
jokes.explanation: The running gag of everyone independently arriving at the car service idea works because it underlines that Dennis's 'innovation' is actually just an Uber. His incomplete 'Why does everyone...' is a great cut-off.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: This is like all foam.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Dee, you goddamn bitch!

jokes.text: Dee in a makeshift beard cut from the Paddy wig: 'The Fighting Irish! That's what Irish people do — they get drunk, they fight people.'
jokes.setup: Dennis told Dee not to wear the stereotype costume; she cut the wig into a beard instead
jokes.punchline: Dee has simply created a different offensive Irish stereotype, now cosplaying as a fighting drunk Irishman, with zero self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Dee's workaround completely misses Dennis's actual objection. The fact that she thinks a fake beard is different from the wig is a great character-stupidity joke.

dialogue.line: Customers trying to call cops, gang confiscating phones

jokes.text: Customer asks: 'So is this like a bang bus?' Dennis: 'No, no, no, no, no. It's not a bang bus.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is trying to explain the Paddy Wagon is an innovative bar experience
jokes.punchline: The van's design apparently resembles a 'bang bus' (pornographic van) enough that a stranger immediately makes the connection
jokes.explanation: The 'bang bus' question is a great dirty non-sequitur that retroactively reframes the whole Paddy Wagon concept. Dennis's 'no, no, no, no, no' — five denials — implies the resemblance might not be entirely coincidental.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: We just drove the snakes out of Philly, the way St. Patrick did.

jokes.text: Dennis walks customers through QR code → app → Facebook login → 30-second ad → online order → prompt service, insisting it's simpler than cash
jokes.setup: Real customers are in the wagon wanting beers
jokes.punchline: The 'streamlined' system is six steps long, the customers just want to pay cash, and Dennis cannot process this
jokes.explanation: Payoff of the payment system joke. Funnier now that real people are rejecting it. 'I don't want you to have my personal information' is a sharp, true detail that lands.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: So, what you're saying is, technically, we gave those guys a very authentic St. Paddy's Day experience.

jokes.text: God, take it easy, Frank! / Don't tell me how to drive, you bitch. / Let's keep it light for the customers, all right, Frank?
jokes.setup: Dennis is trying to deliver a smooth, professional pitch to captive customers.
jokes.punchline: Frank's driving is apparently terrifying, and when Dennis protests, Frank calls him a 'bitch' — which Dennis then has to paper over in front of the customers.
jokes.explanation: Frank insulting Dennis mid-sales pitch and Dennis pivoting to 'let's keep it light' is a good cringe moment. Standard IASIP gang dysfunction material.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Irish honor system... It's an ancient Irish tradition. Know your history, bro.

jokes.text: Dennis can't get the internet to work for his presentation and offers free 'freemiums' to compensate
jokes.setup: Dennis's entire tech-forward business model depends on the internet
jokes.punchline: He has no signal in the van; his innovation crumbles to 'just give them free beers' — called 'freemiums' to maintain the illusion
jokes.explanation: Dennis rebranding free beer as 'freemiums' to save face is excellent character writing. The startup vocabulary applied to 'just give them beers because nothing works' is a sharp joke about tech-bro culture.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I captured a leprechaun, okay? You wouldn't say, 'I kidnapped Bigfoot,' right? You'd say, 'I captured Bigfoot.'

jokes.text: Dee serves beer that is all foam; Dennis: 'Dee, you goddamn bitch!' Frank: 'Keep it light, you bitch!'
jokes.setup: Dennis is trying to maintain a professional, pleasant atmosphere for customers
jokes.punchline: Both Dennis and Frank screech variations of 'bitch' at Dee in front of customers, the van bouncing around, beer all foam
jokes.explanation: 'Keep it light, you bitch!' is the standout line — the contradiction of the content vs. the delivery is funny. Frank using 'bitch' as his standard register while ostensibly trying to be professional is very Frank.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: 'Cause the basement door was locked, so unless he's a being who's unrestrained by the laws of the physical world, he's not getting down here, man.

jokes.text: Customers want to leave, find the door is locked, one calls the cops, Dennis: 'Why would you call the cops? We're just hanging out, man!'
jokes.setup: Customers are trapped in a moving van with people screaming at each other
jokes.punchline: Dennis is baffled why anyone would call the cops on what he genuinely perceives as a fun hangout
jokes.explanation: Dennis's total inability to understand why being locked in a van is alarming is pitch-perfect sociopath comedy. 'We're just hanging out, man!' from someone who locked the door and took their phones is great.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Are you now or have you ever been a leprechaun?

jokes.text: Hey, it's locked. Can you guys let us out? / No, I'm not gonna let you out. Screw this. I'm calling the cops.
jokes.setup: Customers have had enough and want to leave the mobile bar.
jokes.punchline: Dennis refuses to let them out of a locked van — the moment the 'mobile bar' concept tips into kidnapping.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from annoying entrepreneur to actual kidnapper happens naturally and quickly. 'No, I'm not gonna let you out' is terrifyingly casual. This is IASIP's dark escalation at its most effective.

dialogue.speaker: Victim
dialogue.line: No, I'm not a goddamn leprechaun! Please...

jokes.text: Frank orders: 'Push end. Give the phones to the girl.' Then: 'And their money.' Dennis: 'We can't have them cabbing it back to the city and going straight to the cops. That's a good point.'
jokes.setup: Customers try to call cops; Frank responds with swift criminal crisis management
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately pivots to full kidnapping/robbery protocol while Dennis agrees it's logistically sound — both treating it as normal business problem-solving
jokes.explanation: The banality-of-evil joke: 'That's a good point' is Dennis treating crime as a sensible business decision. Frank's operational command voice — 'Push end. Give the phones to the girl.' — is frighteningly competent. The escalation from bar experience to hostage situation in 90 seconds is classic Always Sunny.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You made a wish, which the leprechaun clearly granted.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Don't worry, we're not thieves. You'll get your wallets back, too.' Then immediately: 'And their money.'
jokes.setup: Dennis reassures the kidnapped customers they aren't thieves
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately adds 'And their money' — they are absolutely thieves
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic timing in the script — Dennis's reassurance immediately contradicted by Frank's addendum. 'Don't be babies' after robbing them is a great button.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I wish I could live forever? What are you doing?!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I wish you don't.

jokes.text: Dee: 'Did we just kidnap and rob those guys?' Dennis: 'We just drove the snakes out of Philly, the way St. Patrick did.'
jokes.setup: The gang has just literally kidnapped and robbed their first customers
jokes.punchline: Dennis reframes kidnapping and robbery as an ancient Irish tradition — directly calling back to their earlier wrong history discussion
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Dennis's reframe is both a perfect callback and brilliant comedic logic: they did literally 'drive people out' of Philadelphia. The structure is impeccable — it ties the cold open's absurdist history debate to the kidnapping, retroactively making the earlier scene funnier. 'The way St. Patrick did' lands because we know exactly how wrong their St. Patrick mythology is. This is what the best Always Sunny jokes do: build a premise early and pay it off with something genuinely dark.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I can't tell if you're doing a thing now, or if this is just who you've become.

jokes.text: Did we just kidnap and rob those guys? / We just drove the snakes out of Philly, the way St. Patrick did.
jokes.setup: The gang has just kidnapped and robbed their customers.
jokes.punchline: Dennis reframes kidnapping and robbery as honoring St. Patrick's legacy of 'driving the snakes out' — completing the episode's St. Patrick mythology loop.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. Dennis retroactively justifies their crimes using the gang's own faulty mythology from the opening scene. 'We just drove the snakes out of Philly' is an extraordinary line — it recontextualizes kidnapping as a spiritual act, it completes the thematic loop, and it's delivered with total sincerity. The subsequent domino of everyone accepting this logic ('So, technically, we gave those guys a very authentic St. Patty's Day experience') makes it even better. High quotability, strong rewatch bonus.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Well, if you don't comply with me, then you're gonna end up on the weird one, okay?

jokes.text: Mac's rationalization: 'So technically we gave those guys a very authentic St. Patty's Day experience.' Everyone agrees.
jokes.setup: Dennis has reframed their kidnapping as St. Patrick mythology
jokes.punchline: Mac extends the rationalization to 'authentic St. Paddy's experience' and everyone nods along, satisfied with themselves
jokes.explanation: The group self-satisfaction beat after committing crimes is a great Always Sunny closer for the scene. Everyone being pleased with the 'authentic' experience they provided to people they robbed is dark and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Aw, what's the point, dude? There's no water pressure. I feel like I'm giving him a baby bath.

jokes.text: Mac instructs the bar to operate on the 'Irish honor system' — serve yourselves, put money in a bucket
jokes.setup: Mac is left alone to run Paddy's on St. Patrick's Day
jokes.punchline: He announces an 'Irish honor system' as if it's a real, established thing — it is obviously not and will obviously fail
jokes.explanation: 'Know your history, bro' after inventing an 'ancient Irish tradition' on the spot is a great button. The confidence of Mac's completely made-up cultural authority is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: He probably killed it with his leprechaun magic, anyway.

jokes.text: Beat it! Beat it, Mauricio! I need to talk to Mac.
jokes.setup: Charlie reappears at the bar in the middle of St. Paddy's Day chaos.
jokes.punchline: Charlie dismisses someone named 'Mauricio' — a named background character we never see — with the authority of a man with far more important business.
jokes.explanation: The named but unseen 'Mauricio' is a small absurdist touch. Charlie's urgent dismissal of this person implies a whole offscreen world we don't need to know about.

dialogue.speaker: Victim
dialogue.line: Okay, fine, you got me. I'm a leprechaun... I live in a faraway land, and I was transported here by a giant magical rainbow.

jokes.text: Charlie... what the hell am I looking at? / I caught him. / Wake up that son of a bitch.
jokes.setup: Mac follows Charlie to the basement expecting something mundane.
jokes.punchline: There is a small person in a glue trap. Charlie announces he caught 'him' and tells Mac to 'wake up that son of a bitch' — treating the situation like a wildlife capture.
jokes.explanation: The glue trap payoff is good. 'Wake up that son of a bitch' is the right level of casual menace for Charlie talking about what is almost certainly a human being.

dialogue.speaker: Victim
dialogue.line: And you never got me Lucky Charms.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie & Mac
dialogue.line: (laughing) Oh! That's it! You caught a leprechaun!

jokes.text: Charlie: 'I think you've kidnapped a little person.' Charlie: 'Nah. I've captured a leprechaun. You wouldn't say I kidnapped Bigfoot. You'd say I captured Bigfoot.'
jokes.setup: Mac points out Charlie has kidnapped a small man
jokes.punchline: Charlie's Bigfoot-based legal/semantic argument is completely internally consistent while being completely insane
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The Bigfoot comparison is a genuine logical argument that holds together perfectly in Charlie's framework — the crime changes based on what the captive IS. It's not random; it has internal rules. This is the kind of absurdist character comedy that elevates Always Sunny above shock value. The line is quotable, shareable, and reveals deep character: Charlie isn't stupid, he's operating in a completely alternate taxonomy of reality. Easy 8+ on craft.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Dude, he's talking about that gay bar down on Locust Street-- the Rainbow.

jokes.text: Charlie's locked basement logic: 'The basement door is locked, so unless he's a being unrestrained by the laws of the physical world, he's not getting down here, man.'
jokes.setup: Mac says the person is clearly human
jokes.punchline: Charlie's proof of leprechaun identity is that the door was locked — a human couldn't have gotten in, therefore: leprechaun. Airtight.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's locked-room logic is genuinely clever — it mimics real deductive reasoning perfectly. 'A being unrestrained by the laws of the physical world' is a great phrase for Charlie to deploy. The joke works because Charlie is not wrong about the locked door; he's just drawn the insane conclusion. This level of comedic logic construction is what separates great absurdist from random nonsense.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Right. I'm gonna go check it out, alone... you'll be here, alone.

jokes.text: Mac: 'If he's a human being, he's gonna sue the shit out of us. If he's a leprechaun, he's got a pot of gold.' Both pause. 'Well, let's not rule one out over the other.'
jokes.setup: Mac tries to inject legal reality into Charlie's leprechaun plan
jokes.punchline: Mac's own cost-benefit analysis of human vs. leprechaun leads him to also hope it's a leprechaun — the logic is sound if you accept the premise
jokes.explanation: Mac's rationalization is brilliantly structured: he starts from a reasonable legal concern and ends up at the exact same place as Charlie via pure self-interest. 'Let's not rule one out over the other' is the perfect, cowardly, greedy conclusion. Very quotable. This is Mac at his comedic best — moral flexibility driven by greed framed as open-mindedness.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: The business model's flawless. If you knew how to drive and you knew how to serve a goddamn beer, we wouldn't be in this mess.

jokes.text: Mac formally asks the trapped man: 'Sir, I'm gonna ask you a direct question. Are you now or have you ever been a leprechaun?'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie decide to interrogate the man about his leprechaun status
jokes.punchline: The phrasing mirrors McCarthy-era 'Are you now or have you ever been a Communist?' — applied to leprechaun identification
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best-crafted lines. The McCarthy hearing formulation applied to leprechaun interrogation is a genuinely unexpected, sophisticated reference. The phrase 'or have you ever been' implies a history of leprechaun activity — the bureaucratic solemnity of it is perfect. Extremely quotable. High originality for a sitcom joke.

jokes.text: Sir, I'm gonna ask you a direct question. Are you now or have you ever been a leprechaun?
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie have decided to interrogate the captive.
jokes.punchline: Mac phrases the leprechaun question in the precise syntax of a congressional McCarthyite loyalty oath ('Are you now or have you ever been a Communist'), treating mythical creature status as a matter of formal inquiry.
jokes.explanation: The best single line of the episode and arguably of the season. The McCarthy hearing syntax applied to leprechaun interrogation is a stroke of comedic genius — it's specific, surprising, and structurally perfect. 'Are you now or have you ever been a leprechaun?' has all the marks of a classic IASIP quotable: unexpected register, perfect economy, escalating absurdity. This is 8+ territory without question.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: That bitch was dragging us down.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah. She was driving me crazy, man.

jokes.text: The little person screams 'No, I'm not a goddamn leprechaun!' Mac: 'Pretty convincing.' Charlie: 'If he's a leprechaun, that's what he has to say, right?'
jokes.setup: The trapped man clearly and angrily denies being a leprechaun
jokes.punchline: Charlie interprets a denial as evidence of leprechaun identity — an unfalsifiable trap
jokes.explanation: Charlie's unfalsifiable logic — denial = confirmation — is a clever comedic structure. It mirrors real conspiracy thinking, which makes it both funny and slightly uncomfortable. Mac's 'Pretty convincing' is a great understated endorsement of Charlie's insane framework.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, shit. She didn't put the gas cap on.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Oh, is it open for real?

jokes.text: Mac: 'If he's a leprechaun, that's what he has to say, right?' — treating the denial as proof of leprechaun status.
jokes.setup: The trapped man has vigorously denied being a leprechaun.
jokes.punchline: Mac decides that leprechaun protocol requires denial, so the denial is actually confirmation. His logic has become as circular as Charlie's.
jokes.explanation: Mac's unfalsifiable leprechaun logic — where denial proves the claim — is a good beat showing Charlie's delusion spreading to Mac. The structure mirrors conspiracy theory thinking, which gives it an extra layer.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: It ain't a metaphor. I fell asleep, crashed into a wall, the engine burst into flames, and I had to drive it into a river.

jokes.text: Mac: 'I wish we had a hose.' Looks around. 'Oh, shit. There's a hose right here.'
jokes.setup: Mac wishes for a hose to 'blast the truth' out of the prisoner; the wish is casual and conversational
jokes.punchline: A hose materializes — or was always there — and Charlie immediately frames it as a leprechaun wish
jokes.explanation: Beautifully constructed joke. The hose was clearly always there — this is Paddy's basement — but the timing of Mac's wish creates the illusion of magic. Charlie's immediate 'you made a wish which the leprechaun granted' is fast and confident. The joke runs on comedic logic that is internally consistent: they set up three-wish rules, Mac's hose is wish #1.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, you may be a man. You may be a leprechaun. But only one thing's for sure: you're in the wrong basement.

jokes.text: Charlie panics after Mac says 'I wish I could live forever': 'No! I wish you don't. How about that?!' Mac: 'WHY did you do that?!'
jokes.setup: Mac tries to use his second wish to live forever
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately counters with a wish that Mac WON'T live forever — both wasting the wish and revealing Charlie doesn't want to live forever with Mac
jokes.explanation: Genuinely excellent joke. Charlie's knee-jerk 'I wish you don't' — fast enough to override Mac's wish — implies Charlie has thought about this scenario and decided immortal Mac is worse than mortal Charlie. The relationship subtext (Charlie doesn't want to be with Mac forever) is both funny and revealing. Mac's outrage ('And live forever with you?!' being Charlie's implied reasoning) is perfect. The escalating panic is tightly written.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: (chuckles) No, I've tied a leprechaun to a chair, and, uh, yeah, I was gonna cut him to pieces.

jokes.text: The little person: 'Look, I'm not a leprechaun! Just let me out of here, you dickheads!' Mac: 'Ah. I wish there was a way we could just know for sure.'
jokes.setup: The prisoner clearly and repeatedly states he's not a leprechaun
jokes.punchline: Mac, right after the man says this, wishes aloud for a way to know — using the third wish without realizing it, failing to actually resolve anything
jokes.explanation: Mac burning the third wish on 'I wish there was a way to know' while the man is literally telling them is good irony, though it's a bit anticlimactic as a third-wish payoff. The structure is correct but the punch is lighter than jokes 42-43.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: like, 'I'm a pickpocket. I'm a pickpocket. Stop hurting me. I'm not a leprechaun.' And I just thought that was, like, a metaphor for, you know, 'I-I am a leprechaun.'

jokes.text: Mac sends Charlie to check the gay bar 'The Rainbow' for the pot of gold — 'alone' — with increasingly pointed emphasis on the word 'alone'
jokes.setup: The prisoner says the pot of gold is 'at the bottom of the rainbow'
jokes.punchline: Mac interprets this literally as the gay bar on Locust Street and volunteers to send Charlie, specifically alone, with heavy emphasis — the implication being Mac wants to go himself for personal reasons
jokes.explanation: Classic Mac sexuality joke, executed with great restraint. Mac never says why Charlie should go alone — the repeated 'alone' and 'you'll be there, alone' says everything. It's a callback to years of Mac's closeted characterization handled efficiently in a single scene beat.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, the luck of the Irish.

jokes.text: Dee returns in a new costume — this time as an Irish pirate woman, claiming her 'husband did this to me'
jokes.setup: Dennis told Dee her stereotype characters were offensive and inauthentic
jokes.punchline: Dee has escalated to a third character: an Irish domestic abuse victim pirate, with a new accent
jokes.explanation: Third iteration of the Dee costume running gag. The domestic abuse detail is a dark escalation. Dennis's 'I can't tell if you're doing a thing now, or if this is just who you've become' is an excellent line.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, shit, that leprechaun just flew up a rainbow!

jokes.text: Dennis: 'I can't tell if you're doing a thing now, or if this is just who you've become.'
jokes.setup: Dee is in full pirate-abuse-victim costume doing an accent
jokes.punchline: Dennis can no longer distinguish Dee's performance from her actual personality deterioration
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. The joke works on multiple levels: (1) it's a perfect straight-man reaction to Dee's escalating weirdness, (2) it functions as meta-commentary on Dee as a character who has always been a mess, (3) the phrase 'just who you've become' implies this is a natural destination for Dee, not a performance. Maximum economy — 17 words that do enormous character work. This is a 8+ line.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Stop drinking paint, Charlie.

jokes.text: Dennis tries to get trapped female customers to look happy for his website photos while Dee lurks in the background screaming
jokes.setup: Dennis wants happy photos of customers for the website
jokes.punchline: He's photographing clearly terrified customers while Dee in a pirate costume is yelling in the background — 'No need to cover those up. My customers like those. They're like me.'
jokes.explanation: Dennis talking about his customers wanting to see scared women on a website has some dark undertones that are intentional but slightly confused. 'They're like me' is an unsettling Dennis line. The scene is good cringe but not the sharpest execution.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'If you don't comply with me, then you're gonna end up on the weird one, okay? So smile.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is photographing reluctant kidnapped women
jokes.punchline: He threatens them with the existence of a 'weird' website — implying a second, more sinister version of his bar's web presence
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis Reynolds dark comedy — the casual existence of a 'weird' website is deeply unsettling and very Dennis-coded. He says it like a customer service option. This is the Dennis-is-a-serial-killer running mythology paying off in a character-specific, economical way.

jokes.text: Dennis decides to take their wallets AND write enthusiastic Twitter reviews on their behalf — 'which you would have done, had you experienced our business properly'
jokes.setup: Dennis lets the second group of kidnapping victims go
jokes.punchline: He's going to impersonate them on Twitter to write reviews, treating this as a reasonable substitute for voluntary positive feedback
jokes.explanation: Dennis's rationalization that he's just doing the reviews they 'would have' written is good Dennis logic — he's not stealing, he's completing a transaction. The tech-business satire thread continues effectively.

jokes.text: Mac hosing down the prisoner: 'Talk, bitch! I'm blasting you! Come on, leprechaun! Where's the gold?!' Charlie: 'What's the point, dude? There's no water pressure. I feel like I'm giving him a baby bath.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are using the hose to torture a confession out of the prisoner
jokes.punchline: The hose has terrible pressure; Mac's dramatic interrogation is undermined by Charlie's bored observation that it's more of a 'baby bath'
jokes.explanation: 'I feel like I'm giving him a baby bath' is a genuinely excellent line. The contrast between Mac's intense 'Talk, bitch!' energy and Charlie's bored practical assessment is perfectly written. The specific phrase 'baby bath' is an inspired choice — it's so gentle. Great comic economy and character specificity.

jokes.text: Charlie explains why the snake isn't working: 'That's because the snake is dead. Because you put it in a plastic bag and it couldn't breathe.' Mac: 'He probably killed it with his leprechaun magic, anyway.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are using a snake as an interrogation tool; it's not working
jokes.punchline: The snake is dead because Mac put it in a plastic bag; Mac immediately blames leprechaun magic for the snake's death
jokes.explanation: Mac's pivot to 'leprechaun magic' as the explanation for the plastic-bag asphyxiation is a great character beat. It's not stupid — it's self-serving motivated reasoning. The callback to the snake from scene 2 pays off darkly.

jokes.text: The prisoner finally admits to being a leprechaun: 'Okay fine. I'm a leprechaun... I live in a faraway land, transported here by a giant magical rainbow.' Charlie: 'And you never got me Lucky Charms.' Prisoner: 'That's it! You were right!'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie have been torturing the prisoner with a baby-bath hose for a confession
jokes.punchline: The prisoner sarcastically 'confesses' to being a leprechaun with absurd details; Charlie accepts this completely, specifically breaking down over the Lucky Charms reference
jokes.explanation: The Lucky Charms detail is brilliant. The prisoner throws in the most basic cereal-commercial leprechaun reference as obvious sarcasm; Charlie hears it as the authenticating detail he's been waiting for. 'You never got me Lucky Charms' implies a long, unresolved grievance with leprechauns over cereal. Mac's triumphant 'You were right!' after Charlie's random Lucky Charms accusation seals it. Excellent character-specific absurdism.

jokes.text: I live in a faraway land, and I was transported here by a giant magical rainbow. And you never got me Lucky Charms.
jokes.setup: The captive is sarcastically describing a leprechaun origin story to satisfy Charlie.
jokes.punchline: He adds 'And you never got me Lucky Charms' — a genuinely specific grievance that Charlie will interpret literally.
jokes.explanation: The captive is performing sarcastic capitulation; Charlie hears proof. 'You never got me Lucky Charms' is the right absurdist specific grievance — it sounds like something a real leprechaun would complain about.

jokes.text: Mac's sudden full conversion: 'Oh! That's it! That's it! You were right! Dude! You caught a leprechaun! I told you, man! I knew it!'
jokes.setup: Mac has spent the entire scene skeptical that the captive is a leprechaun.
jokes.punchline: Mac hears the obviously fake confession and immediately achieves total religious certainty — switching from complete skeptic to 'I KNEW IT' in one sentence.
jokes.explanation: Mac's instant conversion from skeptic to true believer is a solid character beat. 'I TOLD you, man! I KNEW it!' despite having said nothing of the sort is the kind of Mac self-revision that's consistent with his character (always wanting to be right). Good payoff to the skeptic role he's played.

jokes.text: Mac's conclusion: 'He's talking about that gay bar down on Locust Street... The Rainbow. You know which one I'm talking about, right?' Charlie: 'No.' Mac: 'Right. I'm gonna go check it out, alone.'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to interpret 'the bottom of the rainbow' as a real-world location.
jokes.punchline: Mac identifies the gay bar 'The Rainbow' as the location of the leprechaun's gold — and then very specifically decides to go there ALONE, while emphasizing repeatedly that Charlie will stay here and Mac will be there, alone.
jokes.explanation: Mac's suppressed homosexuality is one of the show's longest-running character threads. His conspicuously over-explained desire to go to the gay bar alone — 'I'll be there, alone. Right. But you'll be here. Great.' — while maintaining that it's purely a gold-seeking mission, is a great piece of Mac character comedy. High character integration because this joke only works as Mac. The payoff (Mac returning covered in glitter) is set up here.

jokes.text: Mac to the prisoner after Charlie leaves: 'We both know there's no pot of gold at that gay bar. So the question is... what to do with the little liar.'
jokes.setup: Mac sent Charlie away on a fake errand to be alone with the prisoner
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately reveals he knows there's no pot of gold — he never believed in the leprechaun — and pivots to quiet menace
jokes.explanation: Mac's cold pivot from 'go check the gay bar, alone' to quiet interrogator is a great character moment. 'The little liar' is a good darkly comic phrase. The reveal that Mac was running a long con on Charlie is funny.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'We haven't made a goddamn penny today. We actually lost money, with all the gas.' Frank: 'Well, it's not my fault. The business model's flawless.'
jokes.setup: The Paddy Wagon business has failed completely
jokes.punchline: Frank insists the business model is flawless while they've made negative dollars — blaming Dennis's driving and Dee's serving
jokes.explanation: Standard Always Sunny blame-shifting. Functional but not surprising. The irony of 'flawless business model' is easy. Gets the job done.

jokes.text: The gang discovers their routine: they've been picking people up, robbing them, and dropping them outside town 'so often' they forgot to even try to sell beer to the last group
jokes.setup: Frank notes they never tried to sell beer to the last group of victims
jokes.punchline: They realize they've developed a full kidnapping-and-robbery routine so efficient they forgot the original business entirely
jokes.explanation: The reveal that they've fully pivoted their business from mobile bar to serial robbery without noticing is a great character moment. The gang accidentally becoming career criminals is perfectly escalated.

jokes.text: Frank suggests the car service idea; Dennis: 'That idea may work.' Frank: 'Thank you.' Dennis: 'You're welcome.'
jokes.setup: Everyone (Mac, customers) has suggested the car service idea throughout the episode and Dennis has dismissed it
jokes.punchline: Frank suggests it again; Dennis says it 'may work' — now that it's framed as his own consideration. 'You're welcome' instead of 'thank you' implies Dennis thinks he's doing Frank a favor by agreeing
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. Dennis says 'you're welcome' to Frank's thanks — a narcissist's tell. He's incapable of acknowledging he was wrong about the car service idea, so he reframes agreeing to it as a gift to Frank. Great character economy.

jokes.text: Frank drives off leaving Dee behind after pretending the gas cap was an issue
jokes.setup: Frank asks Dee to check the gas cap; Dee steps out
jokes.punchline: Frank drives away without her — it was a ruse to dump Dee
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny 'abandon your friend' bit. The setup is clean, the payoff is satisfying. Dennis and Frank agreeing Dee was 'dragging them down' while she was driving them crazy with the costumes is a good button.

jokes.text: Oh! Hey! / Oh, goddamn! / Goddamn it...!
jokes.setup: Frank has tricked Dee into stepping out of the moving van.
jokes.punchline: Dee falls out of / gets left behind by the van. Her exclamations and Frank's are the audio version of a visual gag — Dee abandoned roadside, Frank accelerating away.
jokes.explanation: Classic IASIP physical gag — Dee getting physically disposed of. Frank's 'Goddamn it' implies he may have accidentally hit her or the execution was messier than planned, which adds to the comedy.

jokes.text: Frank and Dennis discussing leaving Dee: 'She was driving me crazy, man.' Then: 'She didn't put the gas cap on.' 'Oh, is it open for real?' 'Big-time.'
jokes.setup: Frank tricked Dee out of the van
jokes.punchline: The gas cap WAS actually left off — the ruse accidentally created a real problem; Frank's scheme backfired on himself
jokes.explanation: The twist that the fake gas cap problem is a real gas cap problem is a good irony beat. 'Big-time' from Frank is a perfect underplayed response to self-caused disaster.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Very funny. Yeah. That bitch was dragging us down.' Frank: 'Yeah. She was driving me crazy, man.' — calm business post-mortem immediately after abandoning Dee.
jokes.setup: Frank has just abandoned Dee on the side of the road by tricking her out of the van.
jokes.punchline: Dennis and Frank immediately fall into calm, satisfied business-review mode about the decision, as though ditching a team member mid-operation is a standard corporate pivot.
jokes.explanation: Functional extension of joke #55. The calm satisfaction is well-played but doesn't add much to the previous beat — this is the same joke stretched a bit.

jokes.text: Dee, back at the bar: 'I can't believe Uber jacks up their prices just because it's a holiday. That's a scam.' Dennis: 'We should have been doing that the entire time.'
jokes.setup: The gang has been kidnapping people instead of running a legitimate car service all episode
jokes.punchline: Dee complains about Uber surge pricing — the legitimate version of exactly what Mac suggested in scene one — while Dennis realizes they should have been doing that exact thing
jokes.explanation: Full payoff of the Uber/car service running gag. The gang spent the whole episode accidentally running a criminal version of Uber while complaining about Uber. Dennis's 'we should have been doing that the entire time' — still not crediting Mac — is perfect. The irony is complete and well-structured.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'We should have been doing that the entire time.' Dee: 'Are you kidding me? That was my whole idea.' Dennis: 'Dee, stop trying to take credit for everything.'
jokes.setup: Dee mentions Uber surge pricing. Dennis says they should have been doing that.
jokes.punchline: Dee correctly identifies that the car service idea (which Mac originally had, which Dennis dismissed) is now being claimed by Dennis as something they should have done — and when Dee also tries to claim it, Dennis tells her to stop taking credit.
jokes.explanation: The credit-stealing loop — Mac had the idea, Dennis dismissed it, now Dennis claims it, now Dee also claims it, Dennis tells Dee to stop — is a nicely compressed character beat about the gang's inability to acknowledge each other. Solid callback structure.

jokes.text: Frank's business metaphor: 'The business hit a wall, went up in smoke, and then went under.' Mac: 'Why are you speaking in metaphors?' Frank: 'It ain't a metaphor. I fell asleep, crashed into a wall, the engine burst into flames, and I had to drive it into a river.'
jokes.setup: Mac assumes Frank is using business metaphors to describe the Paddy Wagon's failure
jokes.punchline: Frank describes literal events: he crashed the van into a wall, it caught fire, and he drove it into a river — these happened to also be perfect business metaphors
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the finest Always Sunny jokes. The structure is perfect: Mac's reasonable misreading of business metaphors ('hit a wall, went up in smoke, went under') followed by Frank's patient literal correction — he literally crashed into a wall, the engine literally burst into flames, he literally drove it into a river. The three elements all serving as both perfect idioms AND literal events is extraordinary writing. The joke rewards careful attention and is utterly quotable. Comparable in structure to the best of the show's callback-reveal jokes. High originality because the layering of literal/figurative is genuinely clever, not coincidental.

jokes.text: Frank explains the wagon's fate: 'It ain't a metaphor. I fell asleep, crashed into a wall, the engine burst into flames, and I had to drive it into a river.'
jokes.setup: Frank says the business 'hit a wall, went up in smoke, and then went under.' The gang assumes he's speaking metaphorically about the business failing.
jokes.punchline: He was being literal. Each phrase was an exact description of a physical event. He literally fell asleep driving, crashed into a wall, the engine caught fire, and he drove it into a river.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is a perfect double misdirection: Frank uses what sounds like business metaphors ('hit a wall, went up in smoke, went under'), the audience and characters assume figurative speech, then Frank clarifies each was literal — and the literalization is perfectly sequential (wall → fire → river). The structure is immaculate: setup as metaphor → 'it ain't a metaphor' → literal explanation that maps perfectly onto the metaphors. Frank's deadpan delivery of catastrophic vehicle destruction as a simple explanation is excellent character comedy. 'I had to drive it into a river' is the crown jewel line.

jokes.text: Return to the basement: Charlie has tied the prisoner to a chair and is about to cut him while 'Stuck in the Middle With You' plays
jokes.setup: Charlie left Mac in the basement with the prisoner
jokes.punchline: Charlie has escalated to a full Reservoir Dogs torture scene — a little person in a leprechaun suit tied to a chair with a knife, soundtracked by 'Stuck in the Middle With You'
jokes.explanation: The Reservoir Dogs reference is well-deployed — it's not just a wink, it contextualizes the horror of Charlie's situation while making it absurdly funny. 'Stuck in the Middle With You' playing for a tied-up little person in a leprechaun costume is a strong visual/audio gag. The rewatch bonus is high because the composition of the shot would be memorable.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'Well, you may be a man. You may be a leprechaun. But only one thing's for sure: You're in the wrong basement.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is about to torture the prisoner for the truth
jokes.punchline: His ominous pre-torture speech lands on the completely baffling conclusion that the prisoner is 'in the wrong basement' — which tells us nothing and is somehow threatening
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines of the episode. The structure is a perfect villain speech that dissolves into complete nonsense: 'you may be a man... you may be a leprechaun... you're in the wrong basement.' The first two clauses set up genuine menace; the third collapses it into absurdity. It makes no logical sense as a threat but is completely true from Charlie's perspective. The delivery presumably mirrors the Reservoir Dogs scene beat perfectly. Extremely quotable, completely Charlie-brained. This is what 8+ looks like.

jokes.text: Dennis walks in: 'It looks like you've tied a little person to a chair and you're gonna torture him.' Charlie: 'No, I've tied a leprechaun to a chair, and, uh, yeah, I was gonna cut him to pieces.'
jokes.setup: Dennis walks in on Charlie's torture setup
jokes.punchline: Charlie corrects only the 'little person' vs. 'leprechaun' framing, then fully confirms the torture plan — the confirmation is the joke
jokes.explanation: Direct echo of the kidnap/capture semantic argument — Charlie again prioritizes the classification of the captive over the moral issue of torturing him. 'And, uh, yeah, I was gonna cut him to pieces' is a great casual aside. The 'uh, yeah' sells it.

jokes.text: Mac: 'What is this? Why are you covered in glitter?' — immediately after telling everyone 'no questions.'
jokes.setup: Mac has just firmly established a 'no questions' policy about his glitter-covered return from the gay bar.
jokes.punchline: Dennis immediately asks why Mac is covered in glitter, violating the no-questions rule. But it's Mac's OWN rule — suggesting even Mac can't quite help but notice.
jokes.explanation: Actually this is Dennis asking, not Mac — a beat where Dennis can't help questioning Mac about the glitter despite the no-questions declaration. Functional but not among the sharper jokes.

jokes.text: Mac returns covered in glitter: 'I would love to answer all of your questions, but there is no time.' Dennis: 'The gay bar?' Mac: 'Again, no questions.'
jokes.setup: Mac went to the Rainbow (gay bar) alone to find the pot of gold
jokes.punchline: Mac returns covered in glitter with a 'no questions' policy — implying he had a significant personal experience at the gay bar he will not be discussing
jokes.explanation: The glitter payoff on Mac's gay bar solo trip is perfectly executed. 'No questions' is a great panicked deflection. The fact that Mac found wallets there (an actual result) gives him an out but the glitter gives everything away. Good callback payoff to the 'alone' bit.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'I thought [the pickpocket's denials] were, like, a metaphor for I am a leprechaun.'
jokes.setup: Mac reveals the prisoner is a pickpocket who kept saying 'I'm a pickpocket, stop hurting me'
jokes.punchline: Charlie interpreted 'I'm a pickpocket' as a metaphor for 'I am a leprechaun' — his interpretive framework is so broken he heard the literal truth as the metaphorical fiction
jokes.explanation: Brilliant inversion of normal comedy logic: Charlie heard the literal truth and interpreted it as metaphor for a fantasy. This is a deeply character-specific, carefully constructed joke. It retroactively reframes every scene where the prisoner denied being a leprechaun — Charlie processed all of it as confirmation. The specificity of 'a metaphor for I am a leprechaun' is perfect Charlie diction. This is what a 8+ looks like: it's character-integrated to a degree only Charlie could deliver, and it has escalating retroactive impact.

jokes.text: The gang decides to keep all the wallets (theirs + the pickpocket's haul) and 'chalk it up as a win.' Dennis: 'Oh, the luck of the Irish.'
jokes.setup: They were going to return the wallets they'd stolen; now they discover the pickpocket also had a bag of stolen wallets
jokes.punchline: Their original crimes and the pickpocket's crimes cancel out morally in their minds, and they congratulate themselves with a St. Patrick's Day cliché
jokes.explanation: 'The luck of the Irish' as a button after a day of kidnapping, robbery, and wrongful imprisonment is a decent dark-irony button. 'Let's not make it a tradition' / 'probably better not to' is a good self-aware group beat.

jokes.text: Charlie looks out the door: 'Oh, shit, that leprechaun just flew up a rainbow!' Dennis: 'Stop drinking paint, Charlie.'
jokes.setup: The pickpocket/prisoner has presumably escaped
jokes.punchline: Charlie sees the man leave and interprets it as a leprechaun flying up a rainbow; Dennis's response is a perfect straight-line non-engagement
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode closer. 'Stop drinking paint, Charlie' is the most economical possible response to 'that leprechaun just flew up a rainbow' — it doesn't engage with the leprechaun, it goes one level deeper to the root cause. The implication is that Charlie is hallucinating the escape as magical because he has been drinking paint all day. It wraps up both the leprechaun plot and the paint-drinking subplot in four words. Extremely quotable. Dennis's flat delivery makes it land harder. This is an episode-closing joke that actually earns its button.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Stop drinking paint, Charlie.' Charlie: 'Huh.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has just announced the leprechaun flew up a rainbow.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's completely flat 'Stop drinking paint, Charlie' — implying he has said this before and expects no compliance — followed by Charlie's noncommittal 'Huh,' which is neither agreement nor disagreement.
jokes.explanation: The economy here is exceptional — 'Stop drinking paint, Charlie' as a final line and 'Huh.' as the final word of the episode are perfect. Charlie's 'Huh' is the right level of non-resolution: not defiant, not agreeing, just slightly acknowledging. The exhausted-parent tone of Dennis's delivery implied by the text is exactly right for the show's closing dynamics.

tmdb_overview: Dennis tries to create an innovative mobile Paddy's pub experience but runs into trouble when customers refuse to cooperate, while Charlie and Mac attempt to catch a thieving leprechaun.
